newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU and Mexico initial interim trade pact.
newsitem.headline: EU and Mexico initial interim trade pact.

text.p: Mexico and the European Union on Wednesday initialled a long-awaited interim accord that paves the way for negotiations to begin early next year on a fully fledged free trade pact.
"This is without doubt a fundamental step," Mexican ambassador to the EU Manuel Armandariz told reporters.

Armandariz said the interim treaty was a clear signal that both sides were committed "to resolving outstanding questions and reaching an ambitious agreement" on trade in goods and services, intellectual property, foreign investment, public procurement, transfer of capital and fair competition.

Mexico's senior economic adviser in Brussels, Armando Ortega, told Reuters the interim deal would send a positive signal to potential foreign investors by guaranteeing that moves towards free trade were now inevitable.

European and Mexican negotiators have been haggling since 1995 over the scope of a new accord on trade, political coordination and economic cooperation to replace a more limited EU-Mexico cooperation pact signed in 1991.
While some obstacles have been removed, other stumbling blocks still litter the path to a deal.
The two sides were for a long time at odds over European insistence that any accord should contain now-standard clauses on human rights and democracy, a demand Mexico has now accepted.
But Armandariz said trade liberalisation issues -- when and how far tariffs should be cut -- were a far greater problem and still had to be solved before free trade talks could start.

The EU was optimistic of clinching a free trade deal within six months but Mexico was more circumspect, the ambassador said. "An agreement as important as this has to be given all the time it needs," he said.

Armandariz said a free trade deal would benefit both Mexico and the EU as bilateral trade has dwindled over recent years, mainly because of Mexico's membership of the North American Free Trade Area (NAFTA).
European exporters have found it difficult to compete against NAFTA members Canada and the United States, who are able to sell goods to Mexico free of punitive taxes and tariffs.
Mexican exports have also struggled against competition from nations which already have preferential trade deals with the EU.
But with Mexico now claiming to be the world's 10th biggest trader, EU companies are keen to win a bigger slice of its $185 billion-a-year market than last year's 6.1 percent.
In 1990, bilateral trade was nearly 11.5 percent of total Mexican trade.
"Mexico, for the EU, is a market it has conquered and could lose. The EU is a market which Mexico is starting to know and wants to conquer," Armandariz said.

Getting better terms of access to the EU market would help Mexico boost existing exports of oil and raw materials and give it more chance of carving out a niche for manufacturing exports such as textiles, car parts, electronics and chemicals, he said.
